Day-by-day breakage — actual vs. estimated

Case question"What's our total expected breakage revenue this month? How does it split between actual and estimated?"

Case question"How has the estimate for a given payment cohort evolved over time as more information became available?"

The last 28 days reconstructed day by day: actual for any payment whose cycle had already closed by that date, the estimate as it stood that day if it was still open — literally what this dashboard would have shown each of those mornings. Filter by segment to see the same evolution for a specific cohort.
Actual — cycles already closed by that date Estimated — cycles still open on that date

Breakage recognition calendar — 28 days back, 28 days forward

Case question"...Estimated breakage for payments still inside their 28-day window, updated daily as the cycle progresses" — for any day, not just today.

How much breakage lands on each calendar day, keyed on the day the cycle closes. Left of today it's the real figure, because those cycles have closed. Right of today it's today's estimate for cycles still open, placed on the close date each one already has — not a forecast: no new payments assumed, and every bar keeps being recalculated daily until its cycle actually closes.
Already recognized — cycle closed, figure is final Scheduled to be recognized — today's estimate, not yet a fact

Estimate accuracy, month by month

Our additionNot one of the case's 3 literal questions — this is the "in production" version of the backtest: instead of checking it once, watch it every month to catch the model degrading over time.

For cohorts that have already closed: what we would have estimated mid-cycle (day 14) versus what actually happened by the end.
Estimated at day 14 Actual final

When do cycles close within the month?

Our additionNot a literal question from the case — but if closures clustered on certain days, today's "actual" breakage would be more reliable on some days of the month than others.

Calendar day of the month each 28-day cycle closes, across the 9,695 historical payments. The dip on day 31 is a calendar artifact (not every month has one), not a real drop in closures.

Does breakage predict churn?

Our additionBreakage alone doesn't say whether it's "free money" (the student sticks around, just didn't use all their hours) or a symptom of churn (the student is leaving). This tells the two apart.

Closed cycles old enough to know for sure whether they renewed (at least 28 extra days since closing), grouped by their breakage rate. Renewal rate = % that did pay for the next cycle.
Renewal at or above the overall rate Renewal below the overall rate
